incidente.resumo: On January 31, 2017 the data directory of GitLab.com's primary database was accidentally removed while engineers rebuilt replication that had broken under high load. The pg_dump backups had been failing and Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers; GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours and database changes made after 17:20 UTC that day were lost. Service was restored from an LVM snapshot taken about 6 hours before the outage, copied from staging.

descricao.texto: The engineer noticed the mistake and terminated the process a second or two later, when around 300 GB had already been removed.
trechos: The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

gatilho.texto: Trying to restore replication, an engineer wiped the PostgreSQL database directory believing it was the secondary; the command ran on the primary.
trechos: Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary.
Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead.

descricao.texto: Replication had stopped and the secondary had to be rebuilt, which requires an empty PostgreSQL data directory. This was done by hand, in a procedure that was neither automated nor properly documented. The post does not say why the command ran on the primary instead of the secondary.
trechos: Why was the database directory removed?
Database replication stopped, requiring the secondary to be reset/rebuilt. This in turn requires that the PostgreSQL data directory is empty.
Restoring this required manual work as this was not automated, nor was it documented properly.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: pg_basebackup waits silently until the primary starts sending replication data; this was not clearly documented, and an engineer thought previous attempts had left files in the secondary's data directory.
trechos: one of the engineers thinks that perhaps `pg_basebackup` created some files in the PostgreSQL data directory of the secondary during the previous attempts to run it.
this is normal behaviour: `pg_basebackup` will wait for the primary to start sending over replication data and it will sit and wait silently until that time.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: A spike in database load, from an increase in spam and a process removing a GitLab employee and their data, stopped replication because the primary removed WAL segments before the secondary could replicate them; without WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually.
trechos: A spike in database load caused the database replication process to stop.
This was due to the primary removing WAL segments before the secondary could replicate them.
This was caused by two events happening at the same time: an increase in spam, and a process trying to remove a GitLab employee and their associated data.
As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The pg_dump backup ran on an application server with no PostgreSQL data directory, so Omnibus defaulted to PostgreSQL 9.2 against a 9.6 database and the backup failed silently; the failure emails were rejected because DMARC was not enabled for cronjob emails, so no one knew backups were failing.
trechos: The `pg_dump` procedure was executed on a regular application server, not the database server.
As a result there is no PostgreSQL data directory present on these servers, thus Omnibus defaults to PostgreSQL 9.2.
This procedure failed silently because it was using PostgreSQL 9.2, while GitLab.com runs on PostgreSQL 9.6.
Unfortunately DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver.
This means we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers, on the assumption that the other backup procedures were sufficient.
trechos: While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The backup procedure was not tested regularly because it had no owner.
trechos: Why was the backup procedure not tested on a regular basis?
Because there was no ownership, as a result nobody was responsible for testing this procedure.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Restoring was slow: copying the data from the staging host to production took around 18 hours because the staging disks were network disks throttled to around 60Mbps.
trechos: Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.
These disks are network disks and are throttled to a really low number (around 60Mbps)
There was no network or processor bottleneck, the bottleneck was in the drives.

passos.texto: The team chose the LVM snapshot created 6 hours before the outage, the only option to reduce data loss (the alternative lost almost 24 hours).
trechos: To recover GitLab.com we decided to use the LVM snapshot created 6 hours before the outage, as it was our only option to reduce data loss as much as possible (the alternative was to lose almost 24 hours of data).

passos.texto: The PostgreSQL data directory was copied from the staging host to production, which took around 18 hours.
trechos: Since copying over and restoring the data directory would be easier we decided to go with this solution.
Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.

passos.texto: On February 1 at 17:00 UTC the GitLab.com database was restored without webhooks.
trechos: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC we managed to restore the GitLab.com database without webhooks.

passos.texto: Webhooks were restored from a separate staging database built from the LVM snapshot without removing webhooks, via a SQL dump of the table; final restoration and checks finished around 18:00 UTC.
trechos: Restoring webhooks was done by creating a separate staging database using the LVM snapshot, but without triggering the removal of webhooks.
This allowed us to generate a SQL dump of the table and import this into the restored GitLab.com database.
Around 18:00 UTC we finished the final restoration procedures such as restoring the webhooks and confirming everything was operating as expected.

passos.texto: Projects created after 17:20 UTC were restored from their Git repositories still stored in the NFS cluster, but only in their most basic form, without issues or merge requests.
trechos: We ran a procedure to restore these projects based on their Git repositories that were still stored in our NFS cluster.
This procedure however was only able to restore projects in their most basic form, without associated data such as issues and merge requests.

perguntas_em_aberto: The exact amount of lost data is hard to estimate; the post estimates at least 5000 projects, 5000 comments and roughly 700 users.

observacoes: The post gives the data-loss window both as 17:20 to 00:00 UTC and as 17:20 to 23:30 UTC. It does not say why the command ran on the primary instead of the secondary.
